title: Detection of Server
summary: This detection strategy covers the compromise of server infrastructure, where an adversary takes over someone else's server and uses it for command and control, staging or traffic relay. It matters because hijacked servers give the actor a stable, reputable looking address that is hard to block, and because the owner of that server is often a third party who cannot see the abuse from their own logs. The telemetry that makes it possible includes cloud audit logs recording identity and access changes on compute resources, authentication logs showing new key pairs or added users, and network sensor data showing servers contacting many peers in a short time. It fails in practice because these signals also describe a normal administrator fixing a broken host, so correlation with change records and with the previous behaviour of the server is essential.

beginner.definition: Server compromise means an attacker takes control of a server that belongs to someone else. They then use it as a base for other attacks. This detection looks for the signs that a server has changed hands.
beginner.whyItMatters: A stolen server gives the attacker a stable home. It also shifts attention away from them, because the traffic comes from a company that looks ordinary. The real owner may not notice for weeks. Detecting the takeover protects the owner and slows the attacker. It also gives your incident team an address to block with confidence.
howItWorks: Cloud providers and operating systems log who changed a machine, such as a new login key, a new administrator or a changed firewall rule.
Those records flow into your SIEM along with the normal behaviour of the server, such as which peers it usually talks to.
The rule looks for access changes made by an unexpected identity or from an unexpected address.
It then checks what the server did next, such as connecting to many external hosts or opening an unusual listening port.
An alert combines the change, the actor and the new behaviour so the analyst can confirm the server has been repurposed.
beginner.example: Think of a door log in an apartment block. The cleaner enters every flat at the same times each week. If the cleaner enters one flat at midnight, and that flat then starts receiving many parcels from strangers, the door log and the parcel record together tell you the flat is being used by someone else.
takeaways: Watch the management path to a server, not only the workload running on it.
A change is only suspicious when combined with who made it and what happened next.
Third party servers matter too, because traffic from them can reach your network.

objectives: Describe how a compromised server is used to hide the origin of later activity
List the access and configuration changes that indicate a host has changed hands
Correlate a management change with new network behaviour on the same host
Assess which third party hosts your environment trusts and how that trust could be abused
Draft a response path for a confirmed hijacked server, including notification of the owner
dataSources: Cloud provider audit logs for identity changes, added key pairs, security group edits and snapshot exports
Linux authentication logs recording new users, authorized key additions and sudo use
Netflow or firewall logs showing a server contacting many distinct external destinations in a short window
Configuration management database entries describing each server's owner, purpose and normal peer set
logic: The pattern is a management level change on a server, such as an added login key, a new privileged user or a modified network rule, performed by an identity that is not the recorded owner, followed within hours by that server talking to many new external destinations or hosting an unexpected listening service. The fields to correlate are the server identity, the acting account, the source address of the change, the time delta and the new destination set. The benign case is a scheduled maintenance window with a ticket and a known administrator, while the malicious case shows an odd hour change, a credential based access method with no multi factor step and a sharp change in connection profile.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Compute host management change followed by new outbound fan out
# logsource:
#   product: aws
#   service: cloudtrail
# detection:
#   selection:
#     eventName:
#       - ImportKeyPair
#       - AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress
#       - CreateAccessKey
#       - ModifyInstanceAttribute
#   filter:
#     userIdentity.arn|in: approved_operations_roles
#     sourceIPAddress|in: bastion_ranges
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: high
falsePositives: A break glass incident where an on call engineer changes an access key at an odd hour to restore a failed service
Migration tooling that refreshes key pairs across a fleet during a planned platform upgrade
A penetration test that adds a temporary administrator account within the agreed scope
Growth in legitimate traffic that makes a content server talk to many new external destinations
tuningNotes: Scope the rule to hosts that carry your management tooling and to server classes that rarely change, then allow list the operations roles and bastion addresses you actually use. Baseline each server's outbound destination count per hour so the fan out threshold is per host rather than global. Narrowing this way loses coverage on noisy host classes such as proxies, so keep a separate lower severity rule for them and review weekly instead of alerting in real time.
